title: Jajau and the First Crown After Aurangzeb

title_i18n.en: Jajau and the First Crown After Aurangzeb

subtitle: How Jajau Lit the Last Century of the Mughals
figure: Bahadur Shah I and Azam Shah
era: Mughal succession war after Aurangzeb, 20 June 1707
moral: A throne inherited by battle inherits the battle's fractures.

sources.citation: Khafi Khan, Muntakhab ul-Lubab, trans. S. Moinul Haq, 1975
sources.note: Near-contemporary Mughal administrative account of post-Aurangzeb politics.

sources.citation: Kamwar Khan, Tazkirat us-Salatin Chaghata, c. 1724-1725
sources.note: Later Persian court account of the succession wars.

sources.citation: William Irvine, Later Mughals, ed. Jadunath Sarkar, 1922; J.F. Richards, The Mughal Empire, 1993
sources.note: Modern source-based synthesis using Persian and European materials.

panels.shot: epic split-panel composition, half showing Muazzam/Bahadur Shah I in armor, half Azam Shah on an elephant, with a hazy battlefield of tents and guns behind them

dialogue.text: In June 1707, on the parched ground of Jajau, Aurangzeb’s own sons turned their guns on each other—and the first crown after him was hammered out of that single day of fire.

panels.shot: wide aerial view over Aurangabad, fading into a stark deathbed interior

dialogue.text: Aurangzeb died far from Delhi, at Aurangabad, in February 1707. His empire stretched from Kabul to the Cauvery, but he left no clear, binding order for who would rule it next.

panels.shot: tight interior split, showing two separate tents, each with a prince hearing the news

dialogue.text: Muazzam, the elder surviving son in the north, and Azam Shah, the younger near Aurangzeb’s bier, each heard the news and each saw, in that silence, a throne.

panels.shot: low-angle view of Azam in the Deccan proclaiming himself emperor before a gathered court

dialogue.text: Azam acted first. Near the corpse of the old emperor, he took the title of Shah Alam, drew Deccan officers to his side, and marched north, convinced speed would crown him.

panels.shot: medium shot of Muazzam in prayerful posture, then leaning over a map with Rajput and Afghan captains

dialogue.text: Muazzam waited, hesitated, then moved. He had once rebelled and been chained by his father, and knew caution, but he also knew that whoever reached Agra and its treasure first would speak as emperor.

panels.shot: broad landscape of north India, arrows on a ghostly map overlay showing both princes racing toward Agra

dialogue.text: Both princes aimed at Agra. Its fort, its mint, and the imperial harem meant legitimacy. Their letters spoke of obedience and duty, but their drums spoke of war.

panels.shot: medium shot on Muazzam’s mixed army, highlighting diversity—Mughal cavalry, Rajput horsemen, Afghan warriors, and a small Sikh contingent in the distance

dialogue.text: Muazzam’s strength lay in alliances. Khafi Khan notes the Mughal, Afghan and Rajput chiefs who backed him; later Sikh chronicles remember a small band of Guru Gobind Singh’s Sikhs marching in wary support.

panels.shot: low-angle on Azam’s war council at a riverside camp, artillery in the background

dialogue.text: Azam brought with him hardened Deccan troops and gunners who had fought the Marathas for years. Kamwar Khan describes his confidence; he believed experience and nearness to the corpse gave him right and strength.

panels.shot: wide shot of the Jajau plain at dawn, both camps faintly visible on opposite banks of the Chambal

dialogue.text: By June they faced each other near Jajau, between Agra and Dholpur. Chroniclers differ over exact numbers, but they agree on this: two royal camps, one narrow plain, and no room for retreat.

panels.shot: close-up on Muazzam’s face inside his tent at night, lit by a small lamp, with a sealed paper bearing Aurangzeb’s hand beside him

dialogue.text: Stories spread that Aurangzeb had once toyed with dividing the empire among his sons. But by Jajau those speculations meant little. As Muazzam knew, in the Mughal house the field, not papers, decided succession.

panels.shot: dynamic wide shot as both armies deploy, dust clouds rising, artillery being positioned

dialogue.text: At dawn on 20 June 1707, they formed for battle. Artillery in the center, cavalry on the wings, elephant corps in front—a familiar Mughal pattern, but this time the foe was family.

panels.shot: medium shot focusing on Azam Shah atop a richly caparisoned elephant, pointing his sword toward Muazzam’s lines

dialogue.speaker: bahadur_shah_i_and_azam_shah
dialogue.text: “Today, brother, the empire itself shall know its master.”

panels.shot: medium shot on Muazzam on horseback, surrounded by mixed contingents, a Rajput chief at his side

dialogue.speaker: bahadur_shah_i_and_azam_shah
dialogue.text: “Hold your ground. Let their pride break on our guns.”

panels.shot: chaotic battlefield wide shot, cannon smoke, cavalry charges, elephants pushing through, but no gore

dialogue.text: Khafi Khan and Kamwar Khan describe a hard, shifting fight. Artillery tore lanes; some wings held, others sagged. Allies watched which way the wind of fortune began to blow.

panels.shot: focused shot near Azam’s elephant as its mahout falters and the beast turns, sowing confusion among his guards

dialogue.text: In the thick of the struggle, Azam’s center faltered. Chroniclers note confusion around his elephant; whether from a wounded driver or broken ranks, order slipped, and with it, the heart of his army.

panels.shot: intense medium shot of Azam and his son still fighting atop their elephants amidst retreating soldiers

dialogue.text: Azam and his son did not withdraw. The Persian accounts agree on this: they fought on as men around them broke, holding to the old Mughal code that a prince should not turn his back.

panels.shot: somber mid-distance shot showing Azam’s fallen elephant in the aftermath, with Muazzam’s troops cautiously approaching

dialogue.text: By evening, Azam Shah and his sons lay dead near Jajau. With them fell their claim. The chroniclers are clear: the line that had marched from Aurangzeb’s deathbed was cut off in a single day.

panels.shot: low-angle wide shot of Muazzam entering Agra Fort in state, but with wary eyes and heavily armed guards

dialogue.text: From Jajau, Muazzam moved to Agra and the imperial ladies. Taking control of the fort and treasury, he assumed the title Bahadur Shah I—victor by battle, emperor in name.

panels.shot: closer shot of Bahadur Shah I on the Peacock Throne, the hall grand yet shadowed, courtiers divided into cautious clusters

dialogue.text: Yet the victory was narrow and the loyalties that made it so were fragile. Irvine and Richards note how each commander watched for reward, and how every province now knew that a prince could fall to his brother.

panels.shot: wide temporal montage: Jajau’s battlefield fading into later scenes of rebellion and faction around the Mughal court

dialogue.text: Jajau opened the last century of the Mughals. A crown won against a brother carried the crack of that first shot within it, and every later struggle in Delhi echoed the day when Aurangzeb’s sons met by the Chambal.
